questions.questionHtml:
Let $M=\left(\begin{array}{rr}\cos \theta & -\sin \theta \\ \sin \theta & \cos \theta\end{array}\right)$ be a $2 \times 2$ matrix, where $\theta=\frac{2 \pi}{5}$, and $I_{2}=\left(\begin{array}{ll}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{array}\right)$.

Which of the following options is equal to $M^{2026}$ ?

  1. $M^{2}$
  2. $M$
  3. $M^{-1}$
  4. $I_{2}$
questions.explanation: Given, \[ M = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{pmatrix}, \quad \theta = \frac{2\pi}{5}. \] This matrix represents rotation by angle \(\theta\). If we multiply rotation matrices, the angles add So, \[ M^k \text{ represents rotation by } k\theta. \] Now, \[ M^5 \text{ represents rotation by } 5\theta. \] But, \[ 5\theta = 5 \cdot \frac{2\pi}{5} = 2\pi. \] Rotation by \(2\pi\) brings us back to the same position. Hence, \[ M^5 = I_2. \] So, we can write 2026 as: \[ 2026 = 5 \times 405 + 1. \] So, \[ M^{2026} = M^{5 \times 405 + 1}. \] \[ = (M^5)^{405} \cdot M. \] \[ = I_2^{405} \cdot M. \] \[ = M. \] Therefore, \[ \boxed{M^{2026} = M}. \] Correct option: \[ {(B)} \]

Let $S_{2}$ be another set which is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ with dimension two. Which of the following gives the area of $S_{1} \cap S_{2}$ ? $16 \pi$ $4 \pi$ $4 \pi^{2}$ $16 \pi^{2}$
questions.questionHtml:
Consider a set $S_{1}=\left\{x=\left(x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}\right)^{T} \in \mathbb{R}^{3} \mid x^{T} x \leq 16\right\}$. Let $S_{2}$ be another set which is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ with dimension two.

Which of the following gives the area of $S_{1} \cap S_{2}$ ?

  1. $16 \pi$
  2. $4 \pi$
  3. $4 \pi^{2}$
  4. $16 \pi^{2}$
questions.explanation: Given: \[ S_1 = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^3 \mid x^T x \le 16\}. \] Now, \[ x^T x = x_1^2 + x_2^2 + x_3^2. \] So the condition becomes: \[ x_1^2 + x_2^2 + x_3^2 \le 16. \] General equation of a sphere centered at origin: \[ x_1^2 + x_2^2 + x_3^2 = r^2. \] Comparing with: \[ x_1^2 + x_2^2 + x_3^2 = 16, \] we get: \[ r^2 = 16. \] Hence, \[ r = \sqrt{16} = 4. \] Also, \[ x^T x = \|x\|^2, \] so the condition \[ x^T x \le 16 \] means \[ \|x\| \le 4, \] i.e., all points whose distance from origin is at most 4. Thus, \(S_1\) is a solid sphere of radius 4 centered at the origin. Since \(S_2\) is a 2-dimensional subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^3\), it represents a plane passing through the origin. The intersection of a sphere and a plane passing through its center is a circle of the same radius. Therefore, the required area is: \[ \pi r^2 = \pi (4)^2 = 16\pi. \] Hence, \[ \boxed{16\pi}. \] Correct option: \[ {(A)} \]

  1. There is exactly one value of $k$ for which the above system of equations has no solution.
  2. There exist an infinite number of values of $k$ for which the system of equations has no solution.
  3. There exists exactly one value of $k$ for which the system of equations has exactly one solution.

questions.explanation: $\left[\begin{array}{cc| c}1 & k & 1\\ k & 1 & -1\end{array}\right]$ $R_2\leftarrow R_2 - k\cdot R_1$ $\left[\begin{array}{cc| c}1 & k & 1\\ 0 & 1-k^2 & -1-k \end{array}\right]$ $R_2\leftarrow -1 \cdot R_2$ $\left[\begin{array}{cc| c}1 & k & 1\\ 0 & k^2-1 & k+1 \end{array}\right]$ Case 1 :- $k = \pm 1$ $k = 1$, Then the last row will be $\left[\begin{array}{cc | c} 0 & 0 & 2\end{array}\right]$, it implies No solutions for the given system. $k= -1 $, Then the last row will be $\left[\begin{array}{cc | c} 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]$, infinite solutions for the given system. Case 2:- $k \neq \pm 1$ Then there will be pivot in second column, which gives unique solution for the given system. The answers are $A$ and $D$. questions.questionHtml: Let \(A\) be a \(3 \times 3\) real matrix with \(\text{det}(A + iI) = 0\), where \(i = \sqrt{-1}\) and \(I\) is the \(3 \times 3\) identity matrix. If \(\text{det}(A) = 3\), then the trace of \(A^2\) is \(\underline{\hspace{1cm}}\).
questions.explanation: Given that \(\text{det}(A + iI) = 0\), therefore \(A + iI\) is not invertible. This implies that \(i\) is an eigenvalue of \(A\). Since \(A\) is a real matrix, the complex eigenvalues must come in conjugate pairs. Therefore, the eigenvalues of \(A\) are \(i, -i\), and another real eigenvalue . We are also given that \(\text{det}(A) = 3\). The product of eigenvalues is equal to the determinant, so the product of the eigenvalues of \(A\) is \(3\). Since \(i\) and \(-i\) are conjugate pairs, their product is \(|i|^2 = 1\). Therefore, the real eigenvalue must be \(3\). Now, the eigenvalues of \(A\) are \(i, -i, 3\). The trace of \(A\) is the sum of its eigenvalues, so \(\text{trace}(A) = i + (-i) + 3 = 3\). The trace of \(A^2\) is the sum of the squares of the eigenvalues of \(A\): \[\text{trace}(A^2) = i^2 + (-i)^2 + 3^2 = -1 - 1 + 9 = 7\] Therefore, the trace of \(A^2\) is \(7\). rajveer43 answered Jan 10, 2024 • edited Jan 10, 2024 by rajveer43 rajveer43 comment Share Follow See a

Suppose \(M = LU\), where \(L\) and \(U\) are lower triangular and upper triangular square matrices, respectively. Consider the following statements:

\(P\): If each element of the main diagonal of \(L\) is 1, then \(\text{trace}(U) = 3\).

\(Q\): For any choice of the initial vector \(x^{(0)}\), the Jacobi iterates \(x^{(k)}\), \(k = 1,2,3, \ldots\), converge to the unique solution of the linear system \(Mx = b\).

Then
 

(A) both 𝑃 and 𝑄 are TRUE

(B) 𝑃 is FALSE and 𝑄 is TRUE

(C) 𝑃 is TRUE and 𝑄 is FALSE

(D) both 𝑃 and 𝑄 are FALSE

questions.explanation: \(P\): If each element of the main diagonal of \(L\) is 1, then \(\text{trace}(U) = 3\). When a matrix is decomposed into LU form, the diagonal elements of the lower triangular matrix \(L\) are always set to 1 to facilitate the forward elimination process. In this case, if all diagonal elements of \(L\) are 1, then the diagonal elements of \(M\) will be identical to the diagonal elements of the upper triangular matrix \(U\). Therefore, the trace of \(U\) (sum of diagonal elements) will be equal to the trace of \(M\). The trace of \(M\) is \(2 + 3 + 1 = 6\). So, statement \(P\) is FALSE. \(Q\): For any choice of the initial vector \(x^{(0)}\), the Jacobi iterates \(x^{(k)}\), \(k = 1,2,3, \ldots\), converge to the unique solution of the linear system \(Mx = b\). The Jacobi iteration method only guarantees convergence for diagonally dominant matrices, meaning the absolute value of any diagonal element must be greater than the sum of the absolute values of the other elements in its row.
